Update-MgUser -UserId $user.Id -AccountEnabled:$false     # 1. disable
Revoke-MgUserSignInSession -UserId $user.Id                 # 2. revoke refresh tokens

# Exchange: forwarding on the mailbox, then every rule including hidden ones
Get-Mailbox -Identity omar@corp.example | Format-List Forwarding*Address,DeliverTo*
Get-InboxRule -Mailbox omar@corp.example -IncludeHidden |
  Format-List Name,Enabled,RedirectTo,Forward*,Identity
blocks.caption: PowerShell. Export rule details to the case file before removing anything.

blocks.md: Misconception: "we reset the password, so the attacker is out". A reset leaves forwarding rules, registered MFA methods, OAuth consent grants and app passwords in place, and already issued access tokens keep working for up to about an hour in apps without CAE. Disable, revoke, then hunt for each kind of persistence.

blocks.prompt: The UAL search for New-InboxRule on Omar's mailbox returns nothing for Monday to Thursday, but Get-InboxRule shows a forwarding rule created Monday. How can both be true?
blocks.reveal: Several ways, and the report should say which was checked: the UAL entry may not have been searchable yet (Microsoft allows up to 24 hours); the rule may have been created through a different interface that logs under another operation name (for example `UpdateInboxRules` when a client such as Outlook changes rules, or `Set-InboxRule`); or auditing for that mailbox action may not have been enabled. The rule object itself, with its creation details, is the evidence that exists. Absence of a log line is not evidence that nothing happened.

blocks.question: After Omar's account is disabled and Omar's sessions revoked, which attacker foothold is most likely to keep working?
options: The phishing proxy's stolen refresh token
A new interactive sign-in with Omar's old password
A forwarding rule the attacker created on Omar's mailbox, which keeps sending incoming mail outside
The access token, for the next 90 days
blocks.explain: Revocation invalidates Omar's refresh tokens and disabling blocks new sign-ins. Microsoft notes that disabling sign-in also cuts off an app that reads Omar's data through Omar's consent grant. A mailbox rule is different: it runs on the server whenever mail arrives and keeps forwarding until someone removes it. Access tokens last about an hour, not 90 days.

blocks.question: Which mailbox setting sends every incoming message to an external address, separately from any inbox rule?
options: ForwardingSmtpAddress
DeliverToMailboxAndForward
IncludeHidden
IsAdminConsent
blocks.explain: Microsoft documents that a non-blank ForwardingSmtpAddress forwards mail to an external recipient. DeliverToMailboxAndForward only controls whether a copy also stays in the mailbox; IncludeHidden is a parameter of Get-InboxRule; IsAdminConsent belongs to consent audit records.

lessons.title: Uber 2022: from one contractor's login to the cloud consoles

blocks.md:
*Logging and detection engineering* used Uber's September 2022 breach to teach correlation rules for MFA fatigue. Here we follow the same intrusion past the login, because it shows how one identity can reach the cloud consoles without touching a single cloud credential directly, and what a cloud responder must do about it.

**What Uber said** (security update, 19 September 2022): a contractor's account was compromised; the attacker had likely bought the contractor's password on the dark web after malware infected the contractor's personal device. Repeated login attempts sent two-factor approval requests until the contractor accepted one. The attacker "then accessed several other employee accounts which ultimately gave the attacker elevated permissions to a number of tools, including G-Suite and Slack". Uber attributed the attack to the group **Lapsus$**, which the US Cyber Safety Review Board (CSRB) later described as a loosely organized, extortion-focused group active from late 2021 into 2022 that included several juveniles.

**How the access spread, from other sources.** The CSRB's review of Lapsus$ lists, among the group's techniques, "privileged credentials embedded in a PowerShell script, stored on a misconfigured network share", citing an analysis of the Uber breach. Contemporary reports filled in the claimed details: GitGuardian (a secrets-detection company) wrote that one script contained credentials for an administrator of Uber's **PAM** (privileged access management) system, Thycotic, and that from there the attacker showed access to AWS, Google Cloud, Google Drive, Slack and other tools. [Ars Technica](https://arstechnica.com/information-technology/2022/09/uber-was-hacked-to-its-core-purportedly-by-an-18-year-old-here-are-the-basics/) reported screenshots showing access to Uber's AWS and G Suite accounts.

These cloud-console details come from the attacker's own screenshots and messages as relayed by researchers and press, not from Uber. Uber said it had "not found that the attacker accessed any customer or user data stored by our cloud providers (e.g. AWS S3)". A responder's report must keep that line between claims and confirmed findings.

blocks.title: One identity to many consoles (Uber 2022, as reported)

scenes.caption: The entry point: a contractor's identity. Password bought after an infostealer infection; push MFA approved after repeated requests.
Inside the network, a PowerShell script on a file share held credentials for an administrator of the PAM vault (as reported by GitGuardian; the CSRB names the technique).

A PAM vault stores the credentials for everything privileged. Its administrator can reach each one: cloud consoles, collaboration tools and security tools such as Uber's HackerOne bug bounty console (per GitGuardian).
For the cloud responder, every credential the vault held is now suspect, whether or not logs show it used. Uber's response rotated keys to many internal services and forced re-authentication.

blocks.md: **Scoping a breach like this: blast radius.** When an identity, vault or SSO (single sign-on) account falls, the scope is not "what the logs show it touched" but "what it *could* reach". A graph walk over "can reach" relationships (group memberships, SSO app assignments, cloud roles mapped to identity provider (IdP) groups, secrets in vaults) lists everything to check and rotate. The example below is synthetic.

blocks.caption: Python, breadth-first search over a synthetic access graph. Run with python3.

blocks.code:
0 contractor (IdP)
1 VPN
1 wiki
1 file share
2 script with PAM admin password
3 PAM vault (admin)
4 AWS console
4 GCP console
4 Slack admin
4 build secrets
5 S3 buckets
5 IAM
blocks.caption: Output: the hop count is how many steps from the first compromised identity.

blocks.md:
**What Uber did**, in its own words: identified compromised or possibly compromised employee accounts and "either blocked their access to Uber systems or required a password reset"; "disabled many affected or potentially affected internal tools"; "rotated keys (effectively resetting access) to many of our internal services"; "locked down our codebase, preventing any new code changes"; required employees to re-authenticate when tools came back; and added monitoring. Customer-facing services stayed up.

**For the cloud side of such an incident:**

- *Investigate:* CloudTrail `ConsoleLogin` events and IAM Identity Center sign-ins in the window, by which federated identity and from where; Google Admin Activity logs for IAM changes; the PAM vault's own audit log for which secrets were viewed or checked out.
- *Contain:* disable the IdP account and revoke its sessions; for AWS roles reached through SSO, revoke active role sessions (lesson 14); rotate every credential the vault held, starting with cloud administrators.
- *Prevent:* phishing-resistant MFA, or push number matching as an interim step where that is not yet possible, as CISA advised after push-fatigue attacks; no credentials in scripts; PAM administrators as separate, tightly monitored accounts.

Misconception: "the CloudTrail logs show no data access, so the cloud was not affected". If an attacker held a vault administrator account, every stored credential must be treated as exposed. Absence of use in the logs you have narrows the impact; it does not remove the need to rotate.

blocks.question: A PAM vault administrator account was compromised for three hours. Logs show the attacker viewed 4 of the vault's 300 secrets. What should be rotated?
options: Only the 4 secrets viewed
None, if the vault's audit log is complete
All 300 secrets, prioritising the 4 viewed and any cloud administrator credentials
Only the vault administrator's own password
blocks.explain: An administrator could export or reveal secrets in ways the audit trail may not fully capture, and could create persistence. Treat everything reachable as exposed, rotate the confirmed four and the most powerful first, then the rest.

blocks.question: In your report on an incident like Uber 2022, how should the attacker's screenshots showing an AWS console be described?
options: As confirmed access to customer data in AWS
As irrelevant, because screenshots can be faked
As proof that S3 data was downloaded
As claimed access: evidence that a console session existed, to be confirmed or ruled out against CloudTrail and the IdP's logs
blocks.explain: A screenshot is a claim with some weight: it suggests a session existed. The responder checks it against sign-in and API logs and reports what is confirmed separately from what is alleged. Uber, for example, said it had not found access to user data stored with its cloud providers.

lessons.title: Snowflake 2024 and SaaS platforms: hunting from the customer's side

blocks.md:
*Security operations: alert triage and investigation* showed what Snowflake customers could see in 2024. Now take the responder's seat: Mandiant (Google Cloud's incident response and threat intelligence firm) has just told you that records from your data warehouse are for sale. You have no servers to image and no CloudTrail for this product. What evidence exists, how far back does it go, and what do you do in the first day?

Recall the facts from Mandiant's report on the group it tracks as **UNC5537**: every incident it handled traced to stolen customer credentials, mostly from infostealer malware (some infections dated to November 2020); the affected accounts had no MFA, credentials unrotated for years and no network allow lists. Mandiant and Snowflake notified about 165 potentially exposed organisations. Mandiant found no evidence of a breach of Snowflake's own enterprise environment. In shared-responsibility terms, this was the customer's layer.

**The evidence a SaaS product gives you is whatever it chose to log.** Snowflake exposes views in the `SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE` schema. Three matter here:

- **LOGIN_HISTORY**: each login attempt with `CLIENT_IP`, `REPORTED_CLIENT_TYPE` (which Snowflake notes "is not authenticated"), `FIRST_AUTHENTICATION_FACTOR`, `SECOND_AUTHENTICATION_FACTOR` (NULL if no MFA was used) and `IS_SUCCESS`. Snowflake documents latency "up to 120 minutes" and retention of 365 days.
- **SESSIONS**: one row per session, including the client environment (application name, OS).
- **QUERY_HISTORY**: every query and command, joined to sessions and logins.

Mandiant's follow-up hunting guide (June 2024) builds its hunts by joining these three, and notes that default retention lets you hunt across the past year.

Snowflake has since closed the main gap: its strong-authentication rollout, enforced per account from August to October 2026, stops human users signing in with a password alone and blocks password sign-in for service users. New password-only rows should now be rare; 2024 history has many.

**What UNC5537 left in those views**, per Mandiant: logins through the web UI, the SnowSQL command line and an attacker utility Mandiant tracks as FROSTBITE, often from Mullvad or Private Internet Access VPN addresses; recon with `SHOW TABLES` and, per the hunting guide, many `SHOW GRANTS` queries to check access before reading; then staging and exfiltration with a fixed pattern: `CREATE TEMPORARY STAGE` (a **stage** is a named location for loading and unloading data files; a temporary one disappears when the session ends), `COPY INTO` the stage with GZIP compression, and `GET` to download the files. Mandiant also published the client application IDs it saw, such as `DBeaver_DBeaverUltimate`, `JDBC 3.13.30` and `SnowSQL 1.2.32`.

The temporary stage is gone, but the queries that created and filled it are still in QUERY_HISTORY. The two hunts below run on a toy copy of the views in SQLite so you can see the logic and its output; in Snowflake you would run them against `SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE`.

blocks.code:
-- Toy copies of two ACCOUNT_USAGE views (synthetic rows)
CREATE TABLE login_history (event_timestamp, user_name, client_ip,
  second_authentication_factor, is_success);
CREATE TABLE query_history (start_time, user_name, query_text);
INSERT INTO login_history VALUES
 ('2024-04-02 09:01','ETL_SVC','198.51.100.7',NULL,'YES'),
 ('2024-04-03 09:00','ETL_SVC','198.51.100.7',NULL,'YES'),
 ('2024-04-14 10:04','ETL_SVC','203.0.113.66',NULL,'YES'),
 ('2024-04-14 08:30','ANA','192.0.2.10','DUO','YES');
INSERT INTO query_history VALUES
 ('2024-04-14 10:06','ETL_SVC','SHOW TABLES'),
 ('2024-04-14 10:31','ETL_SVC','CREATE TEMPORARY STAGE crm.public.tmp1'),
 ('2024-04-14 10:33','ETL_SVC','COPY INTO @crm.public.tmp1 FROM (SELECT * FROM crm.public.customers)'),
 ('2024-04-14 10:52','ETL_SVC','GET @crm.public.tmp1 file:///tmp/'),
 ('2024-04-14 11:00','ANA','SELECT count(*) FROM crm.public.customers');
.headers on
-- Hunt 1: password-only logins from an IP this user never used before
SELECT l.event_timestamp, l.user_name, l.client_ip FROM login_history l
WHERE l.is_success = 'YES' AND l.second_authentication_factor IS NULL
  AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM login_history p WHERE p.user_name = l.user_name
    AND p.client_ip = l.client_ip AND p.event_timestamp < l.event_timestamp);
-- Hunt 2: the staging pattern Mandiant described
SELECT start_time, user_name, substr(query_text, 1, 28) AS query
FROM query_history WHERE query_text LIKE 'CREATE TEMP%STAGE%'
   OR query_text LIKE 'COPY INTO @%' OR query_text LIKE 'GET @%';

blocks.code:
event_timestamp|user_name|client_ip
2024-04-02 09:01|ETL_SVC|198.51.100.7
2024-04-14 10:04|ETL_SVC|203.0.113.66
start_time|user_name|query
2024-04-14 10:31|ETL_SVC|CREATE TEMPORARY STAGE crm.p
2024-04-14 10:33|ETL_SVC|COPY INTO @crm.public.tmp1 F
2024-04-14 10:52|ETL_SVC|GET @crm.public.tmp1 file://
blocks.caption: Output. The first login row is a false positive: it is simply the earliest row in the data, so it has no history to compare with.

blocks.title: Hunt 1 row by row: password-only logins from a new IP

scenes.caption: Four successful logins. Hunt 1 keeps rows with no second factor whose IP this user never used before.
Row 0: ETL_SVC, no MFA, and no earlier rows exist, so the IP is new by default. It is flagged: a false positive caused by the start of the data window.
Row 1: same user, same IP (IP-A) as the day before. Not flagged, even though MFA is missing: the hunt looks for change, not for the weakness itself.
Row 2: ETL_SVC from IP-B (203.0.113.66), never seen before, password only. Flagged, and the queries that follow from that session staged and downloaded the customers table.
Row 3: ANA used a second factor (DUO), so the first condition already excludes it.

blocks.md:
**First-day response for a SaaS data platform**, combining Mandiant's guidance with the general method of this course:

1. **Preserve**: export LOGIN_HISTORY, SESSIONS and QUERY_HISTORY for the full retention window now, to your own storage, before anything ages out.
2. **Contain**: disable or reset the affected users, rotate their credentials, enforce MFA, and add a **network policy** (by default Snowflake accepts connections from any device; a network policy's allowed list limits where requests may come from).
3. **Scope**: from the flagged sessions, list every query; the tables in `COPY INTO` and `SELECT` statements are your exposure list.
4. **Look outward**: which laptops held these credentials? Mandiant found infostealer infections on contractor laptops also used for gaming and pirated software, and warns that one such laptop can give access to several organisations.

**The same pattern in other SaaS products.** In August 2025 Google Threat Intelligence [described](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/data-theft-salesforce-instances-via-salesloft-drift) UNC6395 using stolen OAuth tokens of the Salesloft Drift integration to export data from many companies' Salesforce instances, then searching the stolen records for AWS keys (`AKIA`), passwords and Snowflake tokens. Salesloft and Salesforce revoked all of the Drift app's access and refresh tokens on 20 August 2025. Google's advice to customers: review the integration's authentication activity and Salesforce's query logs, search your own SaaS data for secrets, and rotate whatever is found. A third-party app's token is an identity; it needs the same logging, scoping and revocation as a user.

Misconception: "the vendor was not breached, so this is the vendor's problem". In both Snowflake 2024 and Salesloft Drift 2025, the evidence, the containment levers (users, network policies, tokens, secrets) and the exposure decision sat with each customer.

blocks.question: Your Snowflake QUERY_HISTORY shows `CREATE TEMPORARY STAGE`, then `COPY INTO @stage` from the customers table, then `GET @stage` from a session that logged in without MFA from a new IP. The stage no longer exists. What can you conclude?
options: Nothing, because the stage was deleted with the evidence
The customers table was very likely staged and downloaded; scope the exposure to it and to anything else that session queried
Only that someone ran a backup
That Snowflake itself was breached
blocks.explain: A temporary stage disappears when its session ends, but the commands that created, filled and downloaded it remain in query history. Together with the new-IP, password-only login, that is the exfiltration pattern Mandiant described.

blocks.question: Why does Hunt 1 flag the very first login in the data even though it was legitimate?
options: Because the service account had no MFA
Because 198.51.100.7 is on a threat list
Because the hunt compares with earlier rows, and the first row in the window has no history, so every IP looks new
Because SQLite handles NULL differently from Snowflake
blocks.explain: "Never seen before" is relative to the data you have. At the start of the retention window everything is new, so baselines need a warm-up period or a separate list of known addresses.

lessons.title: Containing without breaking production, and a cloud IR runbook

blocks.md:
The stolen credentials belong to the role your checkout service runs as. Revoke every session of that role and checkout fails for every customer until the service refreshes its credentials. Leave them and the attacker keeps reading your data. Cloud containment is mostly this trade-off, made under time pressure, with the attacker using the same identities as production.

AWS's Security Incident Response Guide sorts containment into three kinds, and naming them helps you pick the least disruptive one that works:

- **Source containment**: filter where requests may come *from*: security group rules, bucket policies that allow only your VPC endpoint or addresses, WAF IP sets.
- **Technique and access containment**: limit *what identities can do*: remove permissions, deactivate or delete access keys, revoke temporary credentials.
- **Destination containment**: cut off the *target*: network ACLs, shutdown, an isolation VPC, detaching from autoscaling and load balancers.

**Revoking sessions precisely.** *Cloud security and IAM* showed the console's "Revoke active sessions", which attaches a policy denying every session of the role issued before that moment. The mechanism is the condition key `aws:TokenIssueTime`, "the exact time at which the temporary security credentials were created", which AWS says is present only in requests signed with temporary credentials. The model below shows what that does to an attacker and to production.

blocks.caption: Inline policy on the role, shape from AWS's revoke-sessions documentation.

blocks.code:
from datetime import datetime, timezone
UTC = timezone.utc

# Deny every session of this role issued before the cut-off (aws:TokenIssueTime)
CUTOFF = datetime(2026, 3, 4, 2, 40, tzinfo=UTC)

def decide(session):
    if session["issued"] < CUTOFF:
        return "DENY  (issued before cut-off)"
    return "allow (normal policy evaluation)"

sessions = [
    {"who": "attacker copy of app session", "issued": datetime(2026, 3, 4, 2, 5, tzinfo=UTC)},
    {"who": "app, same session",            "issued": datetime(2026, 3, 4, 2, 5, tzinfo=UTC)},
    {"who": "app, refreshed at 02:41",      "issued": datetime(2026, 3, 4, 2, 41, tzinfo=UTC)},
]
for s in sessions:
    print(f"{s['who']:30} {decide(s)}")
blocks.caption: Python model of that Deny condition. Run with python3.

blocks.code:
attacker copy of app session   DENY  (issued before cut-off)
app, same session              DENY  (issued before cut-off)
app, refreshed at 02:41        allow (normal policy evaluation)
blocks.caption: Output

blocks.md:
Two consequences follow. **Production blips**: the legitimate service is denied too until its SDK fetches fresh credentials, so pick a moment and have the owners ready to restart or refresh. **The attacker may simply refresh too**: if they still have code running on the instance, they fetch new credentials from the metadata service after the cut-off, and the revocation achieved nothing. So contain the *source* in the same window: patch or isolate the workload, require IMDSv2, rotate the role's trust if needed.

The same logic applies to IAM users. AWS's guide notes there is no console button to revoke temporary credentials an IAM user created from its long-term key; you attach the same `aws:TokenIssueTime` deny to the user, or delete and recreate the user. Deactivating an access key can be undone; deleting it cannot, so deactivate first, delete after the investigation.

blocks.title: A coordinated containment window (minutes after the decision)

scenes.caption: Minutes 0 to 10, preserve before anyone acts: export logs, snapshot volumes, capture memory (lessons 9 and 10). The attacker is still active and unaware.
Minute 10, all at once: close the source (isolate the workload, IMDSv2), revoke the role's sessions, deactivate stolen keys. Doing them together avoids tipping off the attacker one step at a time.
Minutes 10 to 12: production sees denied calls until its SDK refreshes credentials. The owners were warned; the blip is planned. The attacker's retries fail.
Minutes 13 onward: hunt for persistence (new users, keys, roles, trust policy edits, Lambda changes, shared snapshots) with the lesson 7 rules, and watch for the attacker's next attempt.

blocks.md: **A cloud IR runbook, all lessons in one list.**

1. **Before**: organization trail and aggregated sinks into a separate log account, long retention, data events and resource logs for sensitive stores, EKS audit logs, SaaS audit exports; GuardDuty, Defender for Cloud or SCC on; responder roles provisioned with least privilege "in advance", as AWS advises, and tested; a forensics account; customer managed KMS keys so snapshots can be shared; rehearsed playbooks.
2. **Detect and scope**: walk identity chains back to their origin (lesson 2), list what each credential could reach, note which logs were off.
3. **Preserve**: logs, snapshots, memory, Kubernetes and SaaS records, before the platform deletes them.
4. **Contain**: source, then access, then destination, in one coordinated window; identity incidents also revoke sessions and remove consents, rules and MFA methods.
5. **Eradicate and recover**: remove every persistence item, rotate everything exposed, rebuild workloads from known-good images.
6. **Report**: separate confirmed findings from claims and from what missing logs prevent you from knowing.

**Practise legally.** Only test cloud accounts and tenants you own or have written permission to test, and use a separate, empty account so mistakes cost nothing real.

- [flAWS 2](http://flaws2.cloud/) by Scott Piper: its Defender path gives you "logs of a previous successful attack" to investigate as an incident responder.
- [Stratus Red Team](https://stratus-red-team.cloud/) by Datadog: "detonate offensive attack techniques against a live cloud environment" (yours), mapped to ATT&CK, such as stopping a trail or sharing an EBS snapshot. Run one, then check whether your lesson 7 rules fired.
- [CloudGoat](https://github.com/RhinoSecurityLabs/cloudgoat), Rhino Security Labs' "Vulnerable by Design" AWS deployment tool: attack your own lab, then reconstruct it from CloudTrail.
- Cloud and Microsoft 365 investigation scenarios on [Blue Team Labs Online](https://blueteamlabs.online/) and [CyberDefenders](https://cyberdefenders.org/); check each platform's free tier.

Contain in one coordinated window: close the source, revoke sessions and keys, cut the destination if needed, with production owners ready for the blip. Revocation without closing the source lets the attacker fetch fresh credentials; closing the source without revocation leaves stolen ones working.

blocks.question: You revoke all sessions of an EC2 instance's role, but the attacker still has a web shell on that instance. What happens next?
options: The attacker is locked out for good, because revocation is permanent
The attacker's code fetches new role credentials from the metadata service, issued after the cut-off, and carries on
The instance can no longer get any credentials until AWS support resets it
The attacker can only read, not write
blocks.explain: The TokenIssueTime deny only blocks sessions issued before the cut-off. The instance keeps receiving fresh credentials, and so does any code running on it. Isolate or rebuild the workload in the same window as the revocation.

blocks.question: An attacker used an IAM user's leaked long-term key to create temporary credentials with GetSessionToken. Which action stops those temporary credentials?
options: Deleting the S3 bucket they read from
Rotating the role's trust policy
Nothing; temporary credentials cannot be stopped before they expire
Attaching an inline policy to the user that denies requests whose aws:TokenIssueTime is before now (or deleting and recreating the user), and deactivating the key
blocks.explain: AWS's guide says there is no console option for revoking an IAM user's temporary credentials; the TokenIssueTime deny on the user, or deleting and recreating the user, does it. Deactivating the key stops new ones. The user is not a role, so trust policies do not apply.
